summary: Specified experimental ICMP messages that let a host ask what fully qualified domain name belongs to an IP address. It was an alternative to doing a reverse lookup in the Domain Name System. It is now historic and is listed as obsoleted by RFC 6918.

eli5.summary: You know a house number and want to know the family name. This asked the network a question to find out the name that goes with a number.

questions: how to get a domain name from an ip address with icmp
what are icmp domain name messages
why was in-addr reverse lookup replaced
subtitle: Two ICMP messages that ask an IP address directly for its own domain name.

tldr.problem: Looking up the name for an IP address through the IN-ADDR part of DNS was unreliable: it was not reliably populated, its delegation had fragmented, it was hard to update securely, and its servers were swamped with queries.
tldr.mechanism: A host sends an ICMP Domain Name Request (type 37) to the address in question, and that address answers with an ICMP Domain Name Reply (type 38) carrying its fully qualified domain names and a cache time.
tldr.outcome: This is an Experimental, individual proposal. It is now Historic and listed as obsoleted by RFC 6918.

today: RFC 1788 is Historic and is listed as obsoleted by RFC 6918. It was published as an Experimental protocol and never specified an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why Reverse Lookup Needed a Change
sections.content:
The IN-ADDR domain of the DNS was specified to turn an address into a domain name, and to help find all gateways on a network. The memo says neither function has been remarkably successful, and gives several reasons.

  • The IN-ADDR domain is not reliably populated.
  • Routers are now found with ICMP Router Discovery Messages (RFC 1256) instead.
  • With classless routing and aggregation, the IN-ADDR delegation has fragmented and needs overlapping administration. Reverse administration often does not follow the forward tree, which is not suited to cooperative secure updating.
  • Application servers that want the name for user interaction and security logging have inundated IN-ADDR servers, causing long user-visible pauses when sessions start.

An IESG note says this is an individual product of the author and shows one view of the problem, not a working group result.
sections.eli5: The big phone book that turns numbers into names was often out of date and too busy. So this idea was to ask the house itself what its name is.

sections.title: Direct Query Instead of a Tree
sections.content:
The proposal is that each unicast address be queried directly for its domain name. The naming is then under the same administration as the address assignment, and the queries are spread out the same way IP routing is. In effect, routing is used to index the database.

It is not useful for multicast addresses, because a query to a multicast address could cause a storm of replies and most groups are not named. A request received with a broadcast or multicast destination MUST be silently discarded. The IN-ADDR method SHOULD continue to be used for the well-known multicast range 224.0.0.0 to 224.0.255.255. Other multicast addresses are left for further study.
sections.eli5: Instead of looking up the number in a book, you knock on the right door. You do not knock on a whole crowd of doors at once, because everyone would answer together.

sections.title: How Names Are Written
sections.content: A domain name is a series of labels. Each label is a one-octet length followed by that many octets, and the name ends with a zero length byte for the root. The top two bits of a length octet are 00, so a label is 63 octets or less. When the top two bits are 11, the length is a 2-octet offset used for message compression as described in RFC 1035. The whole name, including length bytes, is limited to 255 octets to simplify implementations.
sections.eli5: Each part of a name is written as a count followed by the letters, and a count of zero says the name is finished.

sections.title: The Request and Reply Messages
sections.content:
The messages use the normal ICMP datagram format, with Type 37 for the Domain Name Request and Type 38 for the Domain Name Reply. A request has Type, Code (0), Checksum, Identifier and Sequence Number. The identifier and sequence number help match requests to replies, and may be zero. A separate request is used for each destination queried.

The reply has the same fields, with the identifier and sequence number copied from the request, then a Time-To-Live and zero or more fully qualified names. The TTL is the number of seconds the name may be cached, and for historic reasons it is a signed two's-complement number. If no name is known the names field is empty, but the reply is still sent as an authoritative statement that no name is known. If several names are known, all SHOULD be listed, and a name that does not fit entirely within the reply MTU is not sent.

The IP source of a reply MUST equal the IP destination of the request. Every host and router MUST implement the server function, and a host SHOULD offer an application interface for diagnostics. After an ICMP error, an implementation MAY fall back to the IN-ADDR method.
sections.eli5: You send a small note saying what is your name, and the house sends back its name or names, and how long you may remember them. If it has no name, it says so clearly.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: A main purpose is to give address-to-name resolution that is more secure than the IN-ADDR reverse tree, and the mechanism can use the IP Security Protocols for authentication and privacy. The routing path does not itself provide security, but it is at least as reliable as delivery of other traffic with the same peer. A DNS cryptographic signature, found by using the reply in the forward DNS direction, can be used to verify the reply.
sections.eli5: You can check the answer by looking the name up the normal way and making sure it points back to the same house.
